lessonTitle: Analgesic Pharmacology: Opioids, Paracetamol, NSAIDs and Adjuncts

blocks.text: A 78-year-old woman is found drowsy on the ward on the first night after a hip hemiarthroplasty. Her breathing is slow and shallow and her pupils are small. Her chart shows regular oral oxycodone, extra intramuscular morphine, and gabapentin started that evening. Understanding why this combination is dangerous is the heart of analgesic pharmacology.

blocks.markdown: **Three analgesic families (objective 1).** *Opioids* (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, codeine, tramadol) act as agonists at mu opioid receptors, which are G-protein-coupled receptors. Activation lowers cyclic AMP, opens potassium channels and closes voltage-gated calcium channels, hyperpolarising neurons and reducing neurotransmitter release in the dorsal horn and brain. Their effects include analgesia, sedation, nausea, constipation, pruritus, urinary retention, miosis and respiratory depression, because mu receptors in brainstem respiratory centres reduce the response to carbon dioxide. Tolerance and dependence follow repeated use. *Paracetamol* has a central analgesic and antipyretic action, thought to involve cyclo-oxygenase (COX) inhibition in the central nervous system, though the mechanism is not fully settled; it has little anti-inflammatory effect. Its main danger is hepatotoxicity in overdose, when the toxic metabolite NAPQI overwhelms glutathione. *Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs* (NSAIDs: ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen) inhibit COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis, giving analgesia and anti-inflammatory effects. Because prostaglandins protect the gastric mucosa, maintain renal blood flow when volume depleted and support platelet function, the risks are gastrointestinal bleeding and ulceration, acute kidney injury, platelet dysfunction, bronchospasm in some patients with asthma and an increased cardiovascular risk.

blocks.title: Multimodal analgesia
blocks.text: The use of two or more analgesic drugs or techniques with different mechanisms and sites of action, so that effects add or synergise while the dose, and therefore side effects, of each (especially opioids) are kept low.

rows: Respiratory depression, sedation, nausea, constipation, tolerance; morphine metabolites accumulate in renal impairment
Hepatotoxicity in overdose; reduce weight-based dose in low body weight and in liver disease (BNF)
GI bleeding, acute kidney injury, platelet dysfunction, asthma, cardiovascular risk
Calcium channel alpha-2-delta subunit, NMDA antagonism, anti-inflammatory
Sedation and respiratory depression, especially with opioids; evidence varies
blocks.caption: Comparison of the main analgesic drug groups. Check doses against the BNF and local guidance.

blocks.markdown: **The WHO analgesic ladder.** Originally developed for cancer pain and widely used as a stepwise teaching model: step 1, a non-opioid (paracetamol or an NSAID) with or without an adjuvant; step 2, a weak opioid (such as codeine or tramadol) with a non-opioid; step 3, a strong opioid (such as morphine) with a non-opioid. In acute postoperative pain the plan is often started at the level that matches the expected severity and stepped down as pain settles, rather than climbing step by step.

**Multimodal and opioid-sparing analgesia (objective 2).** Regular paracetamol and, where there is no contraindication, an NSAID are the baseline. Local anaesthetic wound infiltration or regional blocks reduce the need for opioids. Opioid is added for breakthrough pain and the lowest effective dose used for the shortest time. Each addition must be matched to the patient: NSAIDs are avoided or used with caution in renal impairment, hypovolaemia, active peptic ulceration and aspirin-sensitive asthma; morphine is replaced or reduced in renal impairment; gabapentinoids add sedation and respiratory depression risk, and regulators have warned about their use with opioids. Non-drug measures (reassurance, positioning, early mobilisation and ice) help.

blocks.title: Converting a weak opioid dose to an oral morphine equivalent
blocks.prompt: A patient takes codeine 60 mg four times a day. Using a conversion in which 10 mg of codeine is roughly equivalent to 1 mg of oral morphine, estimate the daily oral morphine equivalent. (Teaching example; conversion ratios vary by source.)

steps.text: Divide by the conversion factor of 10.

Interpret: this is only an estimate. Ratios differ between references, and when switching between strong opioids incomplete cross-tolerance means the calculated dose is commonly reduced (a reduction of 25 to 50 percent is often quoted) and the patient monitored closely. Check against current BNF and local guidance.

blocks.answer: About 24 mg oral morphine per day; the figure is an approximation to be checked against the BNF and a senior colleague.

blocks.title: Weight-based paracetamol dose in a small adult
blocks.prompt: A 40 kg adult needs intravenous paracetamol. Using a teaching dose of 15 mg/kg per dose (maximum adult single dose 1 g), calculate the dose and say what the weight adjustment achieves.

steps.text: Compare with the standard adult single dose of 1 g: 600 mg is less, so the lower weight-based dose is used.

Explain: dosing by weight in adults who weigh less than about 50 kg reduces the risk of liver injury, because the same fixed dose gives a higher mg/kg exposure. Check against current BNF and local guidance.

blocks.answer: 600 mg per dose (teaching example); check the BNF and local policy for the interval and maximum daily dose.

blocks.latex: \text{Oral morphine equivalent (mg/day)} = \frac{\text{daily dose of other opioid (mg)}}{\text{conversion factor}}
blocks.caption: Illustrative only; conversion factors differ between references and between routes of administration.

blocks.markdown: **Opioid-induced respiratory depression (objective 3).** Risk factors are age, opioid-naive status, high or rapidly escalated dose, renal impairment (morphine), obstructive sleep apnoea, obesity and concurrent sedatives such as benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids and alcohol. The earliest reliable sign is increasing sedation, which appears before the respiratory rate falls; pinpoint pupils, a slow or shallow respiratory rate, snoring, falling oxygen saturation and rising end-tidal or arterial carbon dioxide follow. Oxygen saturation may be maintained by supplemental oxygen while ventilation is failing, so it can hide the problem.

items: Recognise: use a sedation score (such as AVPU or a postoperative sedation score) alongside the respiratory rate, and do not rely on saturation alone.
Stop the opioid and any other sedating drugs and call for help.
Stimulate the patient, open the airway and give high-flow oxygen; support ventilation with a bag-valve-mask if needed.
If respiratory depression persists, give naloxone in small titrated increments according to the BNF and local protocol, aiming to restore adequate breathing rather than full wakefulness.
Monitor closely: naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, so re-sedation can occur and repeated doses or an infusion may be needed.
Review the analgesic plan: reduce the opioid dose, add non-opioid analgesia, and treat the cause.

blocks.title: Why naloxone is not a cure
blocks.text: Naloxone reverses opioids competitively but wears off sooner than morphine or long-acting preparations. Giving too much reverses analgesia abruptly, which can cause severe pain, sympathetic surge and, rarely, pulmonary oedema. Use small increments and observe for re-sedation. Check against current BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: Ranking the warning signs
blocks.text: In exam scenarios the early sign of opioid toxicity is sedation, not a low saturation. A patient who is hard to rouse with a falling respiratory rate has already progressed.

points: Opioids act at mu receptors, paracetamol centrally and NSAIDs by COX inhibition; their risks differ (respiratory depression, hepatotoxicity in overdose, GI bleeding and kidney injury).
Multimodal analgesia combines drugs with different mechanisms so that opioid doses and side effects are reduced.
Opioid conversions are approximations: show the arithmetic, reduce the dose for incomplete cross-tolerance, and check the BNF.

Increasing sedation is the earliest sign of opioid-induced respiratory depression; management is to stop the opioid, support the airway and breathing, give titrated naloxone if needed and monitor for re-sedation.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (eGFR about 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) is dehydrated after bowel surgery. Which regular analgesic poses the greatest risk of acute kidney injury?

options.text: A short course of codeine at standard dose
Local anaesthetic wound infiltration
Ibuprofen
Paracetamol

distractorRationale.a: Codeine's active metabolites can accumulate but it does not directly cause AKI.
distractorRationale.b: Infiltration is not nephrotoxic at safe doses.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal blood flow and can precipitate acute kidney injury in volume depletion.
distractorRationale.d: Paracetamol is generally safe for renal function at appropriate doses.

questions.explanation: In a volume-depleted patient with chronic kidney disease, renal perfusion depends on vasodilatory prostaglandins, and NSAIDs remove this protection. Alternatives such as paracetamol, regional techniques and cautious opioid use are preferred.

questions.stem: Which statement about paracetamol toxicity is correct?

options.text: The antidote is naloxone
Toxicity is caused by inhibition of COX-1 in the stomach
Overdose causes respiratory depression through mu receptors
Overdose saturates the usual metabolic pathways, and the toxic metabolite NAPQI depletes glutathione and damages the liver

questions.correctOptionText: Overdose saturates the usual metabolic pathways, and the toxic metabolite NAPQI depletes glutathione and damages the liver

distractorRationale.a: Naloxone reverses opioids; the antidote for paracetamol is acetylcysteine.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: NAPQI accumulates when glutathione is exhausted.

questions.explanation: At therapeutic doses paracetamol is mainly conjugated, and only a small fraction forms NAPQI which glutathione neutralises. In overdose or with depleted glutathione, NAPQI binds to hepatocytes; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.

questions.stem: Under the WHO analgesic ladder, which of the following belongs to step 2?

options.text: A weak opioid such as codeine (with a non-opioid)
An epidural infusion
Paracetamol alone
A strong opioid such as morphine

questions.correctOptionText: A weak opioid such as codeine (with a non-opioid)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: step 2 is a weak opioid with a non-opioid analgesic.
distractorRationale.b: Epidural infusions are not on the ladder.

questions.explanation: The ladder progresses from non-opioids (step 1) to weak opioids (step 2) to strong opioids (step 3), each with adjuvants as needed. It is a teaching framework, and in acute pain treatment may be started at the level that fits the expected severity.

questions.stem: What is the main rationale for multimodal analgesia?

options.text: Combining agents with different mechanisms gives additive or synergistic analgesia, allowing lower opioid doses and fewer side effects
It guarantees that opioids will never be required
It allows a single drug to be given at a very high dose
It removes the need to assess pain

questions.correctOptionText: Combining agents with different mechanisms gives additive or synergistic analgesia, allowing lower opioid doses and fewer side effects

distractorRationale.a: Correct: drugs acting at different sites combine benefit while limiting dose-related harm.
distractorRationale.b: Opioids may still be needed for breakthrough pain.
distractorRationale.c: High single doses increase side effects.

questions.explanation: Paracetamol, an NSAID, local anaesthetic techniques and adjuncts act at different points in the pain pathway. Their combined effect lets the opioid dose be kept as low as possible.

questions.stem: A patient on regular oxycodone becomes progressively harder to rouse over an hour. The respiratory rate is 12/min and oxygen saturation is 96% on 2 L/min oxygen. Which is the most important interpretation?

options.text: The patient is fine because the saturation is above 94%
Respiratory depression only occurs when the rate falls below 8/min
The patient is simply tired and should be left to sleep
Increasing sedation is an early warning of opioid-induced respiratory depression and needs action now

questions.correctOptionText: Increasing sedation is an early warning of opioid-induced respiratory depression and needs action now

distractorRationale.a: Supplemental oxygen can keep saturation normal while ventilation falls.
distractorRationale.b: Thresholds are not reliable and the key sign is falling consciousness.
distractorRationale.c: Unrousable drowsiness after opioids is a medical concern.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: sedation precedes the fall in rate, and oxygen can mask hypoventilation.

questions.explanation: Opioids reduce responsiveness to carbon dioxide, and sedation appears before the respiratory rate drops. A patient who becomes harder to rouse should have the opioid held and be reassessed urgently, and not be reassured by a normal saturation on oxygen.

questions.stem: A single standard dose of naloxone will reliably reverse the effects of a long-acting opioid for the whole duration of the opioid's action.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, so respiratory depression and sedation can return after the antagonist wears off. Patients must be observed, and repeat doses or an infusion may be required, according to local protocol.

questions.stem: A patient takes codeine 30 mg six times a day. Using a conversion in which 10 mg of codeine is roughly equivalent to 1 mg of oral morphine, calculate the approximate daily oral morphine equivalent in mg. (Teaching example only; check the BNF.)
questions.explanation: The daily codeine dose is 30 x 6 = 180 mg. Dividing by 10 gives 18 mg oral morphine per day. This is an approximation and conversion ratios vary by source.

questions.stem: A 48 kg adult is prescribed intravenous paracetamol at 15 mg/kg per dose (teaching example; the standard adult single dose is 1 g). Calculate the single dose in mg.
questions.explanation: The weight-based dose is 15 x 48 = 720 mg, which is below the usual 1 g adult dose. The weight-based figure is used because the patient weighs less than about 50 kg; check the BNF for the dosing interval and daily maximum.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is found hard to rouse on the second night after a thoracotomy. He is receiving regular oral morphine, paracetamol, and a night-time benzodiazepine given by the nurse. His respiratory rate is 8/min with pinpoint pupils. Outline your recognition and management, and your review of the analgesic plan.
markingGuide: Recognises opioid-induced respiratory depression with a contributing sedative (benzodiazepine) and states risk factors
Stops opioid and other sedatives, calls for help
Airway manoeuvres, high-flow oxygen, bag-valve-mask support if needed
Naloxone in small titrated increments per BNF and local protocol; aim for adequate breathing
Warns about shorter duration of naloxone and re-sedation; monitoring (capnography or sedation scores)
Review analgesic plan: reduce opioid dose, optimise paracetamol and NSAID if safe, regional options, avoid or review concurrent sedatives
questions.explanation: The sequence is recognition, stop the cause, support the airway and breathing, reverse in small increments, then monitor and review. Reversal that is too fast can cause pain and haemodynamic upset.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is having a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Describe a multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesic plan and the factors that would make you omit or modify individual components.
markingGuide: NSAID if no contraindication (renal impairment, ulcer history, aspirin-sensitive asthma, bleeding risk)
Local anaesthetic infiltration at port sites or regional technique
Dexamethasone or other adjunct where appropriate
Opioid for breakthrough at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time
Non-drug measures and reassessment; doses checked against BNF and local policy
questions.explanation: Combining analgesics with different mechanisms lowers the dose and side effects of each. Patient factors such as kidney function, bleeding risk, asthma and body weight decide which components are safe.
